cards.front: A species is {{c1::extinct}} when no living members are left anywhere.
cards.quote: A species is extinct when no living members are left anywhere.

cards.front: After a change in the environment, what can happen to the members of a population?
cards.back: Some die and some live. Living members may reproduce, and some migrate to a new place, where they still have to survive.
cards.why: A species with no members that can survive the change may become extinct.
cards.quote: after a change some members die, some live and may reproduce

cards.front: A forest loses its chestnut canopy trees, but chestnut sprouts still grow there. Is the American chestnut extinct? Explain.
cards.back: No. Extinction means no living members anywhere. Millions of sprouts still grow from old roots.
cards.why: Losing the big trees from one forest is a local loss, not extinction.
cards.quote: The American chestnut is not extinct. Millions of sprouts still grow from old roots.

cards.front: {{c1::Habitat loss}} is the destruction of the place where an organism lives.
cards.back: Example: clearing a forest for houses removes homes for animals that nest in old trees.
cards.quote: Habitat loss is the destruction of the place where an organism lives.
cards.section: Explain: four changes that challenge populations

cards.front: {{c1::Pollution}} is harmful material added to air, water or soil.
cards.quote: Pollution is harmful material added to air, water or soil.
cards.section: Explain: four changes that challenge populations

cards.front: {{c1::Climate change}} is a long shift in the usual weather of a region, such as warmer average temperatures.
cards.quote: Climate change is a long shift in the usual weather of a region, such as warmer average temperatures.
cards.section: Explain: four changes that challenge populations

cards.front: An {{c1::invasive species}} is a living thing brought to a new place, where it spreads and causes harm.
cards.back: The chestnut blight fungus is one.
cards.quote: An invasive species is a living thing brought to a new place, where it spreads and causes harm.
cards.section: Explain: four changes that challenge populations

cards.front: Too much fertilizer washes into a bay. Algae grow and fish run short of oxygen. Which of the four kinds of change is this?
cards.back: Pollution. Harmful material (too much fertilizer) was added to the water.
cards.why: It is not habitat loss, because no place was destroyed.
cards.quote: Pollution is harmful material added to air, water or soil.
cards.section: Explain: four changes that challenge populations

cards.front: How does the chestnut blight fungus kill an American chestnut tree, and why do sprouts still grow?
cards.back: It grows into the bark and makes a canker that can kill the trunk above ground. The roots, safe in the soil, often live and send up sprouts.
cards.why: The new sprouts get infected and die back too.
cards.quote: The roots, safe in the soil, often live and send up new sprouts.
cards.section: Explain: four changes that challenge populations

cards.front: In biology, what is genetic variation?
cards.back: Inherited differences among members of a population. One example is how well each member resists a disease.
cards.quote: Genetic variation means inherited differences among members of a population.

cards.front: Why is a population with more variation in resistance more likely to survive a new disease?
cards.back: It is more likely to have some members that already resist the disease. Those survivors can reproduce and pass on the trait.
cards.quote: When a new disease arrives, a population with more variation in resistance is more likely to have some members that resist it.

cards.front: Two forests meet the same new blight. In forest A the trees differ a lot in resistance. In forest B all trees resist poorly. Which is more likely to keep survivors, and why?
cards.back: Forest A. More variation in resistance makes it more likely that some trees already resist the blight.
cards.quote: When a new disease arrives, a population with more variation in resistance is more likely to have some members that resist it.

cards.front: A population has plenty of variation in size and color, but none in disease resistance. Does that variation help it survive a new disease?
cards.back: No. Variation in other traits cannot stand in for resistance. When a change comes fast, the helpful trait usually has to be there already.
cards.quote: Variation in other traits cannot stand in for resistance.

cards.front: Why can new helpful differences usually not save a species from a fast change?
cards.back: They can appear or arrive from other populations, but often too slowly. When a change comes fast, the helpful trait usually has to be there already.
cards.quote: New helpful differences can appear or arrive from other populations, but often too slowly to save a species from a fast change.

cards.front: Why does having a few surviving members not make a species safe?
cards.back: The survivors must also reproduce. Survivors that do not make offspring cannot pass on their traits.
cards.quote: A few survivors do not make a species safe; they must also reproduce.

cards.front: In a very small population, only two members carry a rare trait. What could happen to that trait?
cards.back: It could disappear by chance, if those two die before they reproduce.
cards.quote: In a very small population, a trait can disappear by chance if the few members that carry it die before they reproduce.

cards.front: In the forest model, you run the same settings three times. Will the three lines be exactly the same? Why?
cards.back: They may differ. The model includes chance, so repeated runs show possible outcomes, not one certain future.
cards.quote: They may differ because the model includes chance. Repeated runs show possible outcomes, not one certain future.
cards.section: Explore: send a change through a forest

cards.front: At White Oak Canyon, Virginia, chestnut was 15.2 percent of 719 canopy trees before 1930 and 0 percent in 1977. By how many percentage points did the share change? Does this show extinction?
cards.back: 15.2 - 0 = a fall of 15.2 percentage points. No. The sample shows local canopy loss, not extinction everywhere.
cards.quote: It fell 15.2 percentage points. The sample shows local canopy loss, not extinction everywhere.

cards.front: In 1977, searchers found 176 sampling points with a sprout nearby in 20 person-hours. In 2021 they found 42 sprouts in 40 person-hours. Which year had fewer finds per person-hour, and why is the comparison rough?
cards.back: 1977: 176 / 20 = 8.8 per person-hour. 2021: 42 / 40 = 1.05 per person-hour. 2021 was lower. It is rough because 1977 counted points, not sprouts.
cards.quote: The comparison is rough because 1977 counted points, not sprouts.

cards.front: Hundreds of millions of small chestnut stems are alive, yet no chestnuts were in the later canopy samples. Why do scientists still worry about the species?
cards.back: Most stems are sprouts that get infected and die back, and few make seeds.
cards.why: Survival also needs reproduction (the rule about survivors that reproduce).
cards.quote: Those sprouts get infected and die back too, a cycle that can go on for decades.
cards.section: Explain: four changes that challenge populations

cards.front: When people, not the environment, choose which trees breed, it is called {{c1::artificial selection}}.
cards.quote: This is artificial selection: people, not the environment, choose which trees breed.

cards.front: Virginia site ratings (1 = dead from blight, 4 = no visible disease): American family GMNEW 2.9, hybrid family D2 3.4. Does this prove hybrids always resist blight better than American chestnuts?
cards.back: No. The difference is 0.5, and each row is one family, not a whole species. D2 was one of the best hybrid families.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that data from one family and one place have limits.
cards.quote: Each row is one family of seedlings, not a whole species, and D2 was one of the best hybrid families.

cards.front: Design a test of whether more variation gives more survivors after a dry spell, using radish seedlings. Why should each variety also be grown alone?
cards.back: Compare pots with three varieties against pots with one variety each, then count seedlings alive after 14 days. Growing each alone means one hardy variety cannot explain the result.
cards.why: Keep constants the same: 30 seeds per pot, soil, pot size, light, water.
cards.quote: Also grow each variety alone, so one hardy variety cannot explain the result.
